name: FlashAttention-4 (Blackwell): tensor memory, 2-CTA MMA, and emulated exponential
arithmetic_intensity: FA-4 is the first attention kernel whose bottleneck moves off tensor cores. Feed-and-speeds per B200 SM at M=N=D=128: tensor cores 8192 ops/cycle, exponential unit 16 ops/cycle, shared memory 128 bytes/cycle. Forward per tile: 1024 tensor-core cycles vs 1024 exp cycles vs 768 SMEM cycles - forward is bound by compute AND exponential simultaneously. Backward (5 chained MMAs): 2560 tensor-core, 1024 exp, 3328 SMEM - backward is bound by SHARED-MEMORY BANDWIDTH, not FLOPs. So the reductions are: (1) shared-memory traffic in backward, via storing transposed intermediates directly into tensor memory in the operand-A layout the dV/dK MMAs consume (removing a shared-memory round trip) and via 2-CTA MMA which roughly halves operand-B shared-memory traffic; (2) SFU exp contention in forward, by splitting exp across hardware MUFU.EX2 and a software Cody-Waite + Horner polynomial on FMA units that would otherwise idle, and by explicitly desynchronizing the two softmax warpgroups so they do not contend for MUFU; (3) non-critical-path work, by moving online-softmax rescaling to a dedicated correction warpgroup and only rescaling when the max jump exceeds a threshold tau (the final output is still normalized by the true final statistics, so output is preserved); (4) register pressure, because UMMA accumulators live in TMEM rather than registers - Hopper-era FA-3's register pressure forced a more serial schedule.
scales_with: tile size (FA-4 uses two 128-token query tiles per CTA)
batch_size (scheduling: LPT ordering and batch-head swizzling into L2-sized sections to fight causal load imbalance)
workarounds: tcgen05 UMMA with TMEM accumulators: largest single-CTA tile 128x256x16 in BF16/FP16, ~2x the largest Hopper WGMMA atom, issued by a single thread (eases register pressure, removes Hopper's spilling pain points)
2-CTA MMA: one UMMA across a CTA pair in a cluster spanning both CTAs' TMEM, up to 256x256x16, halving operand-B shared-memory traffic
DSMEM exchange between the CTA pair to repack dS along the non-reduction axis when 2-CTA splitting conflicts with the dQ reduction axis
Store P in TMEM in stages (rather than holding S and P in registers) and fire the PV matmul once 3/4 of P is written
Distribute exp across MUFU.EX2 and an FMA polynomial approximation (Cody-Waite range reduction, Horner form, Sollya-fitted coefficients)
Conditional online-softmax rescaling to delete small rescale steps from the critical path
Longest-processing-time-first tile scheduling plus L2-sized batch-head swizzling; SPT ordering for the deterministic path
Reuse TMEM columns across stages since five full accumulators do not fit (S and P share one column set, dP/dS/dQ another)
notes:
Hardware scope: the repo states FA-4 is 'written in CuTeDSL and optimized for Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (e.g. H100, B200)'; B200 numbers are the ones quoted. The paper's central argument - that tensor core throughput grows far faster than SFU count and shared-memory bandwidth (BF16 tensor cores go from 1 to 2.25 PFLOPs H100->B200 while SFU count and SMEM bandwidth are unchanged) - is a generational scaling asymmetry that every Blackwell kernel author has to re-derive, and it is the reason FA-4 emulates part of the exponential in software. Where it does NOT apply: SM120 consumer Blackwell cannot run sm100a binaries (see the CUTLASS source record), and 2-CTA MMA requires both CTAs of the pair to stay active for the duration, which constrains scheduling. Reported numbers are author claims: up to 1605 TFLOPs/s BF16 on B200 (71% of utilization), 1.3x vs cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7x vs Triton; deterministic backward reaches ~85-90% of nondeterministic throughput. Note that some of these techniques have flowed back into cuDNN 9.13/9.14, so an engine using cuDNN gets some of this benefit without running FA-4 - a caution against reading a vendor benchmark as a library-specific fact.
